claims: A new law came into effect on December 15, 2025.
The new law removes strict first-generation limits.
Under new rules for citizenship by descent, a person with a parent, grandparent, or great-grandparent who was a Canadian citizen may be eligible if they can prove the connection.
New rules for citizenship by descent include "lost Canadians" who missed out under older restrictive laws.
Applicants for proof of ancestry must provide documentation such as birth certificates, marriage certificates, and baptismal records showing direct lineage.
Naturalization requires first becoming permanent residents.
Naturalization requires living in Canada for at least three years (1,095 days) out of the previous five years.
Naturalization requires passing a citizenship test.
Canada allows dual citizenship with the U.S.
Americans do not need to renounce their U.S. citizenship for Canadian citizenship.
Documentation such as census records and property deeds can prove an ancestor was a Canadian citizen at the time of the applicant's birth.
For children born on or after December 15, 2025, to a Canadian parent born outside Canada, a substantial connection of 1,095 days of physical presence in Canada is required.
U.S. citizens are taxed on worldwide income regardless of where they live.
Canadian residents face Canadian tax obligations.
